data.name: self-improvement-10-digress-non_mutating
data.system_prompt: You are a helpful assistant running in an agent harness. You have access to tools. Use them when they help answer the user; otherwise answer directly. When a tool result comes back, incorporate it into your final answer.

data.text: Give me a list of non-mutating unix commands. Like 'ls' or 'wc'

Here’s a list of common Unix/Linux commands that are **non-mutating by default** — they read, inspect, format, or report data without modifying files or system state:

## File / directory inspection
- `ls` — list directory contents
- `pwd` — print working directory
- `stat` — show file metadata
- `file` — identify file type
- `find` — search for files (read-only unless you add `-delete`, `-exec`, etc.)
- `du` — disk usage
- `df` — filesystem usage
- `realpath` / `readlink` — resolve paths / symlinks
- `basename` / `dirname` — extract path components
- `tree` — display directory tree

## Viewing / searching file contents
- `cat` — print file contents
- `head` / `tail` — first/last lines
- `less` / `more` — pager
- `grep` — search text (read-only unless `-r` with output redirects, etc.)
- `strings` — extract printable strings from binaries
- `od` / `hexdump` / `xxd` — hex/octal dump (read mode)
- `nl` — number lines
- `tac` — reverse lines
- `rev` — reverse characters

## Text processing (to stdout)
- `wc` — word/line/byte counts
- `sort` — sort lines (outputs to stdout; `-o` writes files)
- `uniq` — dedupe/compare lines
- `cut` / `paste` / `join` — column/line operations
- `tr` — translate/delete characters (stdout)
- `sed -n` / `awk` — stream editing/processing when printing, not in-place
- `fold` / `fmt` — wrap/format text
- `column` — tabular formatting
- `pr` — paginate/format for printing
- `diff` / `cmp` / `comm` — compare files
- `base64` — encode/decode to stdout

## System info / status
- `uname` — system info
- `hostname` — host name
- `uptime` — system uptime
- `date` / `cal` — date/time, calendar
- `env` / `printenv` — environment variables
- `id` / `whoami` / `who` / `users` — user info
- `ps` — process list
- `top` / `htop` — process monitor (interactive, read-only)
- `free` — memory usage
- `vmstat` / `iostat` — system statistics
- `lsof` — list open files
- `ss` / `netstat` — socket/network stats
- `ip addr show` / `ip link show` — network interfaces (read-only subcommands)
- `df` / `mount` — filesystem info (plain `mount` just lists)

## Command/program discovery
- `which` / `type` / `command -v` — locate executables
- `whereis` — locate binaries/sources/man pages
- `whatis` / `apropos` / `man` / `info` — documentation

## Networking diagnostics (no local file changes)
- `ping` — ICMP echo
- `traceroute` / `tracepath` — route tracing
- `host` / `dig` / `nslookup` — DNS lookups
- `curl` / `wget` with GET and stdout output only (careful: `-o`/`-O` write files)

## Misc / shell built-ins
- `echo` / `printf` — print text
- `true` / `false` — exit status
- `test` / `[` — condition evaluation
- `seq` — number sequence
- `tar -t` / `unzip -l` / `zipinfo` — list archive contents without extracting
- `readelf` / `nm` / `objdump` / `ldd` — binary inspection

## ⚠️ Important caveat
“Non-mutating” is **usage-dependent**. Many of these commands *can* mutate things with certain flags:

- `find -delete`, `find -exec ...`
- `sed -i` (in-place edit)
- `sort -o file`
- `curl -o` / `wget -O`
- `grep ... > file` (shell redirection)
- `tee` (writes to files — not in the list above)

So the safest way to phrase it: **these commands are non-mutating when used in their default/read-only forms.**
put them in a rust `[&str]` like `["which", "whatis",...]`

```rust
const NON_MUTATING: &[&str] = &[
    "apropos", "awk", "base64", "basename", "cal", "cat",
    "cmp", "column", "comm", "cut", "date", "df",
    "diff", "dig", "dirname", "du", "echo", "env",
    "false", "file", "find", "fmt", "fold", "free",
    "grep", "head", "hexdump", "host", "hostname", "htop",
    "id", "info", "iostat", "join", "ldd", "less",
    "ls", "lsof", "man", "more", "mount", "netstat",
    "nl", "nm", "nslookup", "objdump", "od", "paste",
    "ping", "pr", "printenv", "printf", "ps", "pwd",
    "readelf", "readlink", "realpath", "rev", "sed", "seq",
    "sort", "ss", "stat", "strings", "tac", "tail",
    "test", "top", "tracepath", "traceroute", "tree", "tr",
    "true", "type", "uname", "uniq", "uptime", "users",
    "vmstat", "wc", "whatis", "whereis", "which", "who",
    "whoami", "xxd", "zipinfo",
];
```

Note: a few of these (`find`, `sed`, `sort`, `grep`, etc.) can mutate with certain flags (`-delete`, `-i`, `-o`, `> file`), so the array assumes their default/read-only usage.
